explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Jonah 1:17 says the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah. Jonah just went overboard, and the answer is already on its way. It's a strange kind of help, but the text says the LORD arranged it.

You're thinking ahead, friend. A plant does show up later in this story, when the LORD God appoints one over Jonah (Jonah 4:6). But right here in the water, the text says the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow him. The plant has to wait its turn.

That wind is in the story, but it comes later. God appoints a scorching east wind in Jonah 4:8. Here Jonah is in the sea, and the text says the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow him. Wrong weather, wrong chapter, friend.
Right on the money. Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. That's a long stretch with no windows and no exits. I bet he counted every minute, but that's just my guess.
A full week is a big number, but it isn't the one here. The text says Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. Three days is already plenty to spend inside a fish, baker.

Forty is a number that shows up in other Bible stories, so I see why it came to mind. This one is smaller, though. Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. Forty would be a very different story, friend.

explanations.answer: He prays to the LORD his God
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. From inside the fish, Jonah prayed to the LORD his God. No crowd, no ship, no lifeboat, just Jonah talking to the LORD. Whatever else is going on in there, the text puts the prayer first.

explanations.answer: He falls into a deep sleep
explanations.explanation: Sleep does come up earlier in this story, since Jonah was asleep on the ship during the storm (Jonah 1:5). But here the text says something else. From inside the fish, Jonah prayed to the LORD his God. Different spot, different moment.

explanations.answer: He cries out to the sailors
explanations.explanation: The sailors are behind him now, friend. They're the ones who threw him overboard (Jonah 1:15). Inside the fish, the text says Jonah prayed to the LORD his God. The only one he's talking to is the LORD.

True! Jonah says, “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me.” Then he says that from the belly of Sheol he called for help, and the LORD heard his voice (Jonah 2:2). He's telling the story of a prayer that got answered. That's a good thing to say from inside a fish.

This one is true, baker. Jonah says that from the belly of Sheol he called for help, and the LORD heard his voice (Jonah 2:2). He also says, “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me.” So the prayer looks back on being heard.

Yes, friend. Jonah says to God, “For You cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas.” He speaks directly to the LORD about it. The sailors did throw him over (Jonah 1:15), but in his prayer, Jonah names the LORD.

The fish comes after the deep, baker. In his prayer Jonah says to the LORD, “For You cast me into the deep.” He names the LORD, not the fish. The fish shows up in the story, but Jonah doesn't give it that credit.

The king of Nineveh isn't anywhere near this sea, friend. Jonah hasn't even gotten to Nineveh yet. In his prayer he says to the LORD, “For You cast me into the deep.” That's the answer the text gives.

explanations.answer: Look once more toward God's holy temple
explanations.explanation: Nailed it, baker. Jonah says, ‘I have been banished from Your sight; yet I will look once more toward Your holy temple.’ Notice that little word “yet.” Even in the middle of all that water, he's turning his eyes toward the temple.

explanations.answer: Swim hard for the nearest shore
explanations.explanation: That's what most of us would say, friend. But the text doesn't give Jonah a swimming plan. He says he will look once more toward God's holy temple (Jonah 2:4). His eyes go toward the temple, not toward a shoreline.

explanations.answer: Wait in silence for the sea to calm
explanations.explanation: Silence isn't what Jonah describes, baker. He's in the middle of a prayer, and he says he will look once more toward God's holy temple (Jonah 2:4). He's talking and looking, not just waiting.

explanations.answer: Raised it up from the pit
explanations.explanation: That's the turn, baker. Jonah says the earth beneath him barred him in forever, and then comes the big “But.” “But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God!” He went down to the roots of the mountains, and the LORD brought his life back up.

explanations.answer: Left it down in the pit
explanations.explanation: Down is where Jonah says he went, but that's not where his prayer stops. He says the earth barred him in forever, and then adds, “But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God!” That “But” changes everything, friend.

explanations.answer: Handed it back to the sailors
explanations.explanation: The sailors don't come back into this prayer. Jonah says the LORD raised his life from the pit (Jonah 2:6). He gives the LORD the credit by name. Nobody on a ship is part of that sentence.
That's the word, baker! Jonah says, “As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD.” His life is fading, and the LORD is who he remembers. Then his prayer went up to the LORD's holy temple.
I get why that word came to mind, friend, with all that trouble. But the text says something else. Jonah says, “As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD.” That's the word Jonah uses.
Doubt isn't the word Jonah uses here, baker. He says, “As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD.” Then his prayer went up to the LORD's holy temple. Remembered is what the text gives us.

Close, but it's flipped, friend. Jonah says, “Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion.” So the people holding on to idols are the ones walking away from God's loving devotion. They aren't holding on to it.
Right, baker. Jonah says, “Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion.” They hold on to idols and walk away from God's loving devotion. It's the opposite of what the card said.

You got it, friend! Jonah says, “But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You.” He's still inside the fish when he says it. The prayer started in distress, and here it's speaking thanks.
Mourning fits a dark moment, baker, so I see the pull. But Jonah says, “But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You.” Thanksgiving is the word in the text.

That's the voice a lot of us would use in a spot like that, friend. But Jonah says, “But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You.” The text says thanksgiving, and that's what he promises to bring.

That's the closer, baker. Jonah finishes his prayer with, “Salvation is from the LORD!” It's a short line, but it lands hard. After everything he said about the deep, the last word is that the LORD is where salvation comes from.
Judgment is a word that might come to mind here, friend, after a storm and a fish. But Jonah ends with, “Salvation is from the LORD!” That's how the prayer closes.
Jonah's prayer does go through some dark places, so sorrow makes sense as a guess. But the last line is, “Salvation is from the LORD!” That's the final note of the prayer, baker.

That's right, baker. The LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land (Jonah 2:10). The fish doesn't act on its own here, because the LORD gives the command. It isn't pretty, but Jonah ends up on solid ground. And friend, this story isn't over.

explanations.answer: Spits him onto a passing ship
explanations.explanation: That would be quite a landing, friend. But the text says the LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land (Jonah 2:10). No ship, just ground. The story isn't over yet, either.

explanations.answer: Carries him back out to sea
explanations.explanation: Jonah has already had plenty of sea, baker. The text says the LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land (Jonah 2:10). So the fish takes him to land, not away from it. And the story isn't over yet.
